newsitem.title: FIJI: RTRS - Fiji 1996 sugar crush extended into 1997.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Fiji 1996 sugar crush extended into 1997.

text.p: The 1996 Fiji sugar crushing season will be extended into early 1997 due to rain and mechanical problems at mills, Sugar Commission of Fiji chairman Gerald Barrack said on Monday.
"We would have liked to finish in December, but the two big mills will go into January," Barrack told Reuters.
Crushing at Fiji's four mills started in June and was now half completed with 2.0 million tonnes of cane crushed, he said.
The Commission forecasts between 4.2 to 4.3 millon tonnes of cane will be crushed in 1996, compared with 4.11 million tonnes in 1995.
However, sugar content will again be lower than expected.
"With a slightly lesser tonnage of cane in 1994 we produced a record 517,000 tonnes of sugar," Barrack said.
"This year we have caned possible 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes more, but we are probably going to produce between 460,000 to 480,000 tonnes of raw sugar," he said.
In 1995, Fiji produced 454,447 tonnes of raw sugar.

Barrack said that pre-season testing of cane in 1996 indicated that the sucrose content was comparable to the record 1994 season, but three weeks of rain in June saw the sugar content drop and crushing delayed.
Low sugar content is caused when cane is not given sufficient time to produce sucrose before crushing. Sucrose is produced in sunny conditions.
Barrack said short-term mechanical problems at Fiji's two biggest mills, Lautoka and Labasa, also delayed crushing.
Fiji's smallest mill, Penang, which produces for domestic consumption, is expected to finish crushing in November, with the Ba mill finishing in late December, Barrack said.
But Lautoka and Labasa will crush into January, he said.
Fiji's sugar industry has often been plagued by industrial unrest, but Barrack said the 1996 season had been dispute free.
"I am pleased to say all the wage negotiations were completed ... before the start of the season and we haven't had any industrial problems -- hopefully we won't," he said.
"I don't see anything on the horizon that suggests we will have a problem."
Barrack said on prelimary figures the 1996 season is expected to be worth F$260 million (US$202.8 million) to F$280 million, compared with just over F$300 million in 1995.
